title: Give a Coding Agent the Tools to Build and Verify a Website
summary: Give a coding agent a practical path from a scoped website brief to reviewed assets, working interactions, and an inspectable deployment preview.
body_markdown:
A coding agent can write a website and still fail to deliver a usable result. It may lack approved assets, misunderstand a third-party API, overlook a broken mobile layout, or stop at a successful build. The right tools close those specific gaps between code and a reviewable website.


This guide describes a reference workflow for moving from a brief to a verified preview. A shared service layer can simplify access to research and media capabilities. Repository access, infrastructure accounts, deployment authority, and production approval remain separate responsibilities. No website was generated or deployed as part of this article.


## Define what launch means before granting tools


For a prototype, a launch might mean a private preview that a founder can review on a phone. For a production site, it also involves domain routing, analytics, accessibility, form delivery, privacy requirements, and a rollback plan. Those are different acceptance criteria and permissions.


Write a compact delivery contract: intended visitor, main action, required pages, approved copy sources, visual references, supported viewports, and who may authorize publication. Include a concrete example of the main action, such as submitting an inquiry that reaches a controlled test inbox. “Build a beautiful landing page” leaves too many important decisions implicit.


Then separate preparation from publication. The agent can research, create code, assemble assets, and produce a preview under one permission set. Publishing to a shared domain may require another. This keeps the work moving while preserving a clear decision point for the person responsible for the site.


## Map capabilities to the build


Most website projects need five capabilities: reference research, code editing, asset preparation, rendered inspection, and deployment. They do not all belong in the same service or credential. Your existing coding environment should continue to handle files and builds; a tool platform should supply missing external capabilities.


Work Useful capability Result to retain


Understand an integration Official documentation retrieval Source URL and verified contract


Prepare imagery Approved image or media service Asset, usage rights, generation settings


Inspect layout Browser rendering or screenshots Viewport-specific evidence


Validate interactions Browser and controlled test accounts Actual observed behavior


Share the result Authorized preview deployment Immutable preview URL and build identity


An image generator does not fix an unclear offer. A browser tool does not establish permission to publish. Tool discovery should follow the delivery contract, as described in[choosing an agent’s tools](https://o11.ai/blog/choose-agent-tool-set) .


## Research before writing integration code


Ask the agent to read the existing project before proposing a stack. A functioning application may already have shared components, design tokens, form handling, and analytics. Replacing these to fit a familiar tutorial creates unnecessary work and maintenance.


For external APIs, retrieve current official documentation and verify the exact endpoint, authentication, input, and response. Store the relevant page URL with the implementation notes. A successful example from an older SDK version is not proof that the installed version uses the same method.


Keep a small integration contract for each external service: what input the site sends, what output it expects, what happens on timeout, and which account owns the request. This avoids a common failure where the frontend appears complete but relies on an unconfigured server function or a secret that cannot safely exist in browser code.


Research access is especially useful here because the coding agent can resolve missing details without making the developer open another provider dashboard. The benefit is faster access to evidence. It does not remove the need to inspect the evidence.


## Make assets deliberate and reusable


Choose the visual approach before generating anything. Product UI, diagrams, typography, photography, and illustration serve different purposes. A developer product often benefits more from a precise workflow diagram or actual interface capture than a decorative image.


Give an asset task a specification: placement, aspect ratio, minimum usable size, background, palette, required content, forbidden content, and export format. Keep real product interfaces truthful. A fictional screenshot with nonexistent features can make an otherwise polished page misleading.


Save source settings and the selected asset together. Assign a meaningful filename and describe the image for assistive technology when it conveys information. Record usage rights for supplied photography, logos, fonts, and generated material according to the relevant terms. Avoid asking the agent to imitate another company’s distinctive brand assets.


For generated video or images, wait for a confirmed result and download the artifact before including it in a build. Submission acceptance is not an asset.[The long-running media guide](https://o11.ai/blog/agent-async-image-video-jobs) explains how to preserve those jobs across interrupted sessions.


## Review the rendered site, including its states


A build verifies that the compiler can produce an artifact. It does not establish readable text, working forms, or a sensible mobile layout. Inspect the rendered site at representative desktop and narrow widths, then exercise the main action.


[Playwright supports screenshot comparisons](https://playwright.dev/docs/test-snapshots) , with rendering consistency dependent on the environment. Whether you use automated screenshots or manual inspection, retain the viewport and browser context so reviewers understand what they are seeing.


Review loading, empty, validation-error, success, and server-failure states. A contact form that silently fails under a network error can lose more value than a visual imperfection. Check keyboard navigation, visible focus, readable contrast, image sizing, link destinations, and horizontal overflow. Open the actual output files, not just their names in a directory listing.


Choose checks appropriate to the project. A small static edit may need a build and a visual review. A payment or authentication flow needs deeper functional verification under authorized accounts. The agent should report what was observed and what remains untested rather than treating every passed check as production certification.


## Use previews as the review artifact


Share a versioned preview with a short review note: what changed, which interactions were checked, which configuration is missing, and how to approve publication. The reviewer should be able to examine the exact artifact that would become public.


[Cloudflare Pages supports preview deployments](https://developers.cloudflare.com/pages/configuration/preview-deployments/) . Its documentation also explains preview access controls. Select the appropriate visibility rather than assuming an obscure URL makes a preview private.


Keep preview and production configuration distinct. A preview should not send real customer notifications or mutate production records during a demonstration. Conversely, a preview with mocked data must be labeled so the reviewer does not mistake it for a verified backend connection.


Record the build identifier, environment, and deployment URL. If publication is approved, promote the reviewed artifact where the deployment system supports it, or verify the resulting production build against the same source. Define how to restore the previous working version before changing a shared domain.


## Limit the cost of experimentation


The expensive part of an agent-assisted website is often repeated exploration. Unbounded asset variations, full-site screenshot loops, and repeated deployments can accumulate while the agent searches for a subjective improvement.


Use explicit rounds. For example, authorize three visual concepts, select one, then permit two refinement rounds. Suppose each concept requires four illustrative media calls at an assumed $0.25 per call. Three concepts cost $3 before refinements. That is an example budget, not a provider price or measured project cost. Code editing, inference, hosting, and review time are separate.


For a shared tool layer such as o11, inspect each operation’s current account mode and maximum before execution. Infrastructure accounts may still be required, particularly for customer-owned projects and resources. Consolidating tool access should not make ownership harder to understand.


Use[the full workflow cost worksheet](https://o11.ai/blog/multi-tool-agent-cost-estimation) to include failed generations and discarded assets. Counting only the selected hero image understates the cost of producing it.


## Protect secrets and preserve a handoff


Give the agent scoped credentials for the smallest useful environment. Keep deployment secrets out of screenshots, generated pages, browser bundles, and research prompts.[GitHub’s guidance on preventing data leaks](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/tutorials/secure-your-organization/prevent-data-leaks) includes limiting token permissions and detecting exposed secrets.


If a credential appears in an artifact, revoke or rotate it through the responsible account and inspect the exposure. Deleting the visible string alone does not establish that it was never copied. Record the recovery action without reproducing the secret in the handoff.


Finish with usable deliverables: source, approved assets, setup instructions, required environment variable names, verification notes, preview link, and publication status. Explain unresolved provider configuration plainly. A teammate should be able to maintain the website without reconstructing the agent’s chat history.


The best first version of this workflow ends at a reliable preview. Once that path works, add authorized publication and post-launch checks. Tools make a coding agent more productive when they help it cross a concrete delivery gap and leave behind evidence of the result.


## Example: a reviewable one-page launch


Consider a fictional founder asking for a product page with a demonstration video and an inquiry form. A useful first delivery includes the page source, approved product copy, the selected video file, a narrow-screen capture, and a preview where the form can be checked against a controlled destination.


The agent should identify missing configuration precisely. “The form renders, but delivery credentials are not configured” is a reviewable limitation. A fabricated success notification would conceal the remaining work. Similarly, a generated media thumbnail should not stand in for the actual video file in the preview.


The founder can then approve concrete choices: the offer, layout, demonstration, and form behavior. Publication authority can remain a final decision because the work is already assembled. If the video misses the accuracy standard, the page can use an approved still while the media item is revised.


Keep the handoff tied to the same preview revision. If the agent changes copy or assets after review, reopen the affected decision instead of silently publishing a different result. This makes the tool-assisted workflow faster to collaborate on, because everyone is discussing an inspectable website with known remaining work.
